title: Raga Asa
hookLine: the raga of hope, and the ballad sung while the sky is still dark

cards: Long before sunrise, the street outside a gurdwara is still dark, a dog barks somewhere, and a few cars pull in with their headlights on. Inside, the lights are already up. Someone uncovers a harmonium.
A tabla player taps the drumhead, listening for the pitch. People drift in with their heads covered, sit on the carpet, and the singing begins before the birds do.
What they're singing has a name: the Asa di Var, the ballad in Asa.

teach.b: Raga Asa is the next great section of the Guru Granth Sahib, right after Gauri. In Punjabi, asa is also an everyday word for hope, and Sikh tradition likes to hear that in the raga's name: the raga of hope.
Its mood is described as longing that leans forward, a hope that something good is on its way. That fits the hour.

By Sikh custom the Asa di Var belongs to the morning, sung in gurdwaras while the day is still breaking. A var is a ballad, built of stanzas called pauris, with short verses called saloks set between them.
In this one, the saloks come from Guru Nanak and Guru Angad. Here's one of Guru Angad's, in plain English.

teach.h: A HUNDRED MOONS, A THOUSAND SUNS.
teach.b: If a hundred moons rose, and a thousand suns climbed the sky, with all that light there would still be deep darkness without the Guru.

Heard at dawn, that lands differently. The sun is coming up anyway; the salok says outside light isn't the whole story. There's a light the Sikh Gurus point to that a sunrise can't supply, the light of the Guru's word.
So the ballad is sung right at the edge of morning, while one kind of light is arriving, to ask for the other.
Hope at dawn, then, isn't forced cheer. It's facing the day before it has shown its hand, and starting it with the Word.

how: In gurdwaras the kirtan of the Asa di Var is commonly sung in the early morning, with ragis singing Guru Nanak's pauris and the saloks between them, and the congregation sitting and listening as the day begins.

o: the raga of grief, sung at funerals
the raga of hope, home of the dawn ballad
a night raga for the bedtime prayer

games.q: what's inside raga asa — tap the pairs.
p: a short verse set between stanzas

s: the Asa di Var is usually sung late at night
it belongs to the morning; it's commonly sung while the day is still breaking.
the saloks in the Asa di Var come from Guru Nanak and Guru Angad
the pauris are Guru Nanak's, and the saloks between them come from both Gurus.
Guru Angad's salok says a thousand suns would be enough light
it says even with a hundred moons and a thousand suns, without the Guru there would be deep darkness.

games.q: the sun is about to rise, and a ballad is about to be sung. what does Guru Angad's salok say all that sunlight leaves out?
games.why: a hundred moons and a thousand suns, the salok says, and still deep darkness without the Guru. the outside light arrives anyway; the ballad asks for the other one.

practice: Let your breath slow and picture the sky just before sunrise, not dark, not light, that gray-blue in between.
Let one real hope come up, small or large, for today or for someone you love, and let it sit there in the half-light without polishing it.
If you pray, say Waheguru once and leave the hope with it; if you don't, keep it company quietly.

wordCard.voice: Raga Asa. The raga tradition hears as hope, home of the Asa di Var, the ballad sung while the morning breaks. Today's word.

orig.note: asa, the raga's name, which is also an everyday Punjabi word for hope.

carryVoice: Your line: hope at dawn. One kind of light arrives while the ballad asks for the other. See you tomorrow.
